summary: This informational document lists service requirements for Layer 2 provider-provisioned VPNs. It gives terminology, general requirements, and detailed needs from both customer and provider views, covering point-to-point VPNs (VPWS) and multipoint VPNs (VPLS).

eli5.summary: Before building private lines for customers, you write down what customers and the phone company each need. This is that wish list, for both one-to-one and many-to-many connections.

subtitle: A checklist of what customers and providers need from Layer 2 VPN services that look like a private wire or a shared LAN.

tldr.problem: Service providers were building several different technical approaches to Layer 2 VPNs, and there was no common list of what such a service has to deliver.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC collects requirements from the customer's view, the provider's view and the engineering view, for point-to-point services (VPWS) and LAN-like services (VPLS), and offers them as a checklist for judging each approach.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational document, not a protocol: it does not specify how to build L2VPNs, only what they should do.

today: RFC 4665 is an Informational document, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes requirements as they stood in September 2006 and specifies no protocol.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 4665 gives requirements for provider-provisioned Layer 2 Virtual Private Networks (L2VPNs). It lists features that may apply to one or more of the approaches a Service Provider (SP) could use. The technical specifications for providing the service are explicitly out of scope; the framework in RFC 4664 and other documents cover that, and the terminology comes from RFC 4026.

The document is meant as a checklist: a consistent way to evaluate and document how well each approach meets each requirement. The provider and the customer agree on a Service Level Specification (SLS), which is part of the Service Level Agreement (SLA). A sound L2VPN design keeps the Customer Edge (CE) and the Provider Edge (PE) properly separated so the SLS can be honored.
sections.eli5: This is a shopping list, not a recipe. It says what a good private network service must do, and leaves how to build it to other documents.

sections.title: Two Kinds of L2VPN: VPWS and VPLS
sections.content:
The requirements separate two models by how connectivity is provided. A Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS) makes a pair of CE devices appear connected by a single logical Layer 2 circuit. PE devices act as Layer 2 circuit switches, and the circuits are mapped onto tunnels in the SP network. VPWS applies to Ethernet, ATM, Frame Relay and others.

A Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) makes the CE devices of one VPLS appear connected by a single LAN. Each PE holds a Virtual Switching Instance (VSI) for each L2VPN it serves. The VSI ends the pseudo wires that link it to VSIs in other PEs and the attachment circuits that connect CEs, and it holds the forwarding information base, which can be filled dynamically by source MAC address learning or statically by configuration. IPLS is a variation limited to customer IP traffic.
sections.eli5: A wire service is like a string between two cups. A LAN service is like a big room where everybody in your group can hear everybody else, even though they sit in different buildings.

sections.title: Requirements Shared by Customers and Providers
sections.content:
Section 5 holds the general requirements. A VPLS MUST support unicast, multicast and broadcast traffic, and the service MUST keep the connectivity type of its L2VPN type whatever tunnel topology the provider uses. L2VPN solutions SHALL prevent CEs from interacting with unauthorized entities, must provide traffic separation between L2VPNs, and MUST support overlapping addresses, so customers can use the same MAC addresses in different L2VPNs.

The RFC also admits that a VPLS differs from a real LAN: it is probably less reliable, frames can be duplicated if the pseudo wire sequencing option is off, very late delivery (more than half a second) can hurt, and 802.3x Pause frames are not carried.

Other shared requirements cover QoS (best effort is mandatory; the 'hose' and 'pipe' modes from RFC 3809 are also named), restoration that MUST be faster than the time customer protocols need to detect a failure, standard management interfaces such as SNMP MIB modules, and multi-vendor interoperability.
sections.eli5: Everyone wants the same basics: your traffic stays separate from other customers, it gets where it is going, and if a path breaks it is fixed before you even notice.

sections.title: Customer and Provider Requirements in Detail
sections.content:
Customers need an L2VPN that can span multiple providers yet still look like one homogeneous service, and that gives consistent QoS whichever access technology each site uses. Isolation of traffic and forwarding information should be similar to private lines, Frame Relay or ATM. Access must support multi-homed sites, backdoor links between customer sites and devices homed to two or more providers. In a VPLS, the committed minimum MTU MUST be the same for a given instance, and loops MUST be prevented. CE devices should need only minimal or no configuration.

Providers need unique identifiers for each SP domain and each L2VPN, and discovery so that PEs learn L2VPN membership with little manual configuration. Membership changes should be handled within the provisioning timeframe, typically minutes, and can be as short as the rerouting timeframe, typically seconds. Providers must be able to offer inter-AS and inter-SP L2VPNs, and wholesale one SP's service to another. Resources shared between L2VPNs should be limited so one instance cannot starve the rest. Section 7.14 asks for testing and fault-location tools whose test packets MUST NOT leave the SP network.
sections.eli5: Customers want it to feel like their own private network. Providers want to set it up with little fuss and make sure one customer cannot hog things that others need.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security runs through the whole document. Section 5.5 lists hazards that methods MUST protect against: protocol attacks, resource exhaustion (replication, looping, MAC table limits), unauthorized access, tampering with signaling and tampering with data forwarding. The provider network also MUST be protected against malformed or malicious customer traffic, and its devices MUST NOT be reachable from any L2VPN unless authorized.

Where an L2VPN runs over part of the Internet, the RFC asks for a configurable option to use standard IPsec methods for confidentiality, integrity, authentication and replay prevention. If an L2VPN carried over IP crosses an unsecured network, security mechanisms MUST be employed, and the RFC suggests considering both authentication and encryption for such a tunnel.
sections.eli5: Because many customers share the same equipment, the service has to keep each customer's data apart and lock the doors against attackers.
